transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. Before we start, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Um, I guess what finally pushed me to come in is… at work I keep starting these follow-up things after audits, or after mentoring events, and I really do mean to finish them. Like I’ll draft the email or open the review note or pull up the form, and then somehow days later I’ll realize the final step never happened.

It’s embarrassing, because I’m an accountant, so details are kind of supposed to be my thing. And it’s not that I don’t care—if anything I care too much and then I’ll get pulled into something else, or I’ll think “I’ll just come back to that,” and then… it’s just sitting there unfinished. That’s the main thing that made me think, okay, I probably need to talk to someone.
Thinking back, did you notice similar problems with finishing tasks or staying focused when you were a kid or in school, or is this something that's only become an issue as an adult?

Oh no, it definitely goes back. I mean, I didn’t think of it that way at the time, because I was a good student in some ways—like I could do well on tests, especially if I liked the subject. But even in elementary school my report cards would say things like “bright, but loses assignments,” or that I rushed through and missed little details.

And I talked out of turn a lot, apparently. My mom still brings this up—she’ll joke that I could ace the test and then forget the project that was literally sitting in my backpack. Which is funny now, sort of, but also… yeah, that pattern was there pretty early. I needed reminders to actually finish things and turn them in.
Aside from the focus and follow-through issues, do you notice things like feeling restless, needing to move or fidget a lot, or having trouble sitting still for extended periods?

Yeah, definitely. Sitting still for a long review is… weirdly uncomfortable. Like, I’ll be in a meeting going through workpapers or audit notes, and after a while it feels like this pressure building up inside me, like I have to move or I’m going to crawl out of my skin a little.

So I’ll stand up to go to the printer, or refill my water, or suddenly decide I need a file from across the room—even if I probably don’t. It’s not always obvious, I don’t think, but I’m kind of inventing reasons to get up.
Do you notice these same problems—like losing track of tasks or feeling restless—affecting things outside of work, such as at home or in your personal relationships?

Yes. I mean, work is the obvious one because it’s measurable, you know? Like if I miss a follow-up after a client review, there’s a paper trail, and lately it’s gotten to where an actual client review was affected. That was… awful. And now I’m worried people are looking at me like, “Can she really handle this promotion?” which is humiliating because I worked hard for it.

But at home it’s there too. My husband has basically taken over bills and things I said I’d handle—appointments, commitments, stuff like that—because he can’t really count on me to finish them reliably. And I hate saying that, because I’m not trying to dump things on him. I’ll agree to do something with full intention, and then it just slips or I get halfway through and don’t close the loop.
Have you been experiencing any persistent low mood, excessive worry, or anxiety recently that might be contributing to these difficulties?

I’m not sure. I mean, I worry about work, definitely, but it feels more like… because things are slipping, not the other way around? Like after something goes wrong, then I’m anxious about it.

I wouldn’t say I’ve had a constant low mood, at least not that I’ve really noticed. It’s more frustration and embarrassment. Though sometimes I wonder if I’m just bad at telling the difference, because I’ll be thinking about one missed thing and then suddenly I’m remembering three other things from last month and—sorry, I’m getting off track.

So… no, I don’t think there’s been some persistent depression or anxiety driving it. At least not that I can clearly point to.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others in conversations, blurting out responses before someone finishes speaking, or making quick decisions without fully thinking them through?

Yes… I do. I catch myself jumping in before people are finished, especially with junior auditors. It’s like I can see where they’re going, or I think I know the answer, and it feels weirdly urgent in my head—like if I don’t say it right then, I’ll lose it.

And then I’ll realize I cut them off. Sometimes I try to soften it, like, “Sorry, go ahead,” but by then I’ve already interrupted the flow. It’s embarrassing because I don’t mean to steamroll anyone. I’m just… the thought pops out before I’ve really decided to say it.
Do you regularly use caffeine, alcohol, or any recreational drugs, and if so, how much?

I’m not sure I can give you a clean number off the top of my head. I haven’t really been tracking it, which is probably not very helpful.

I mean, I can try to think through a typical week, but I’d be guessing a bit. If it matters for what you’re assessing, I can pay closer attention and give you a more accurate answer next time.

Have you ever had distinct periods—lasting several days or more—where you felt unusually elevated, euphoric, or irritable, needed much less sleep than usual, and had racing thoughts, separate from your everyday pattern?

I don’t think so… not in a clear way like that. I mean, I have stretches where I’m keyed up or irritable, especially if there’s a deadline or something is messy at work, but several days of feeling euphoric or needing way less sleep—no, I can’t really point to that.

Racing thoughts, maybe? But that feels kind of normal for me when I’m trying to keep track of too many things. Like I’ll be lying there thinking about one email, then a spreadsheet, then whether I forgot to return my sister’s call—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

So… I haven’t noticed distinct periods like you’re describing. At least not separate from my usual pattern.
How would you describe your typical sleep—do you usually get enough hours, and do you wake up feeling rested, or do you struggle with sleep problems like insomnia or excessive daytime sleepiness?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that cleanly. My sleep is… kind of all over the place depending on the week, I think. I don’t always pay attention to the actual number of hours, which is probably something I should know.

Some mornings I’m fine, and other mornings I feel like I’ve been hit by a truck, but then I also wonder if that’s just because I stayed up too late doing random things around the house or looking at something on my phone. My husband jokes that I “putter” at night, which is true, but he also falls asleep in like five minutes, so I don’t know if he’s a fair comparison.

I wouldn’t say I have a clear sleep problem that I’ve really tracked. I just haven’t measured it enough to tell you, honestly.
Would you say these difficulties with focus, restlessness, and impulsivity have been consistently present for at least the past six months, rather than coming and going in shorter bursts?

Yes… I think so. More than six months, definitely. It’s been noticeably getting in my way for, gosh, about almost two years now—maybe a year and ten months?

It really became obvious after I got promoted, after that firm-wide award thing. Which sounds like a good problem, I know, and I was happy about it, but the workload and responsibilities got a lot harder to juggle after that. And since then it hasn’t felt like short bursts so much as this ongoing thing I’m constantly trying to manage.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a lifelong (childhood-onset, confirmed by school reports of losing assignments, missing details, needing reminders) pattern of both inattentive symptoms (fails to complete follow-up tasks, loses track of work, difficulty sustaining attention in meetings) and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (subjective restlessness/urge to move, fidgeting via inventing reasons to get up, interrupting colleagues, blurting out answers). Symptoms are present across multiple settings (work and home), have persisted >6 months (nearly 2 years of clear impairment, with earlier childhood history), and cause clear functional impairment (missed client follow-up, spouse assuming responsibilities, concerns about job performance). Mood symptoms, anxiety, and manic/hypomanic episodes were explicitly screened for and denied, and substance use does not appear to account for the pattern, making combined-type ADHD the best fit over mood or anxiety disorders.
